prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
Quick framing note: I'll answer this as a "time capsule" exercise — using only the market conditions, trends, and information that were actually known as of January 2, 2019, not anything that happened afterward. This isn't personalized financial advice, and beating the S&P 500 over 5 years is something even most professional stock-pickers fail to do.

**Context as of 1/2/2019:** The S&P 500 had just closed out a rough Q4 2018 (a ~20% near-bear-market drop from the September peak), closing around 2,510. Rates were rising, trade-war fears with China were high, and growth/tech names had been sold off hard — creating what many saw as attractive entry points into structurally growing businesses.

Given the themes visible at the time — cloud computing, digital payments, streaming, e-commerce, and SaaS adoption — here are 10 stocks a growth-oriented investor might reasonably have considered:

| # | Company | Ticker | Jan 2019 Rationale |
|---|---------|--------|---------------------|
| 1 | Microsoft | MSFT | Azure was the clear #2 in cloud infrastructure and growing >70% YoY; Nadella-led enterprise/cloud pivot was working; strong balance sheet. |
| 2 | Amazon | AMZN | Dominant e-commerce + AWS (still the largest cloud provider by share); advertising business emerging as a new profit engine. |
| 3 | Alphabet | GOOGL | Search/YouTube ad duopoly with Facebook; huge net cash position; valuation had compressed after the 2018 selloff. |
| 4 | Visa | V | Secular shift from cash to card/digital payments globally; high-margin network with few real competitors. |
| 5 | Mastercard | MA | Same payments-digitization tailwind as Visa, duopoly structure, strong international growth runway. |
| 6 | Adobe | ADBE | Successful shift to subscription (Creative Cloud, Document Cloud) drove recurring revenue and margin expansion. |
| 7 | Salesforce | CRM | Leading cloud CRM platform; had just closed the MuleSoft acquisition to expand its enterprise cloud footprint. |
| 8 | NVIDIA | NVDA | Stock had been cut roughly in half after a 2018 crypto-mining demand collapse and gaming GPU inventory glut — but the underlying data-center/AI/gaming GPU growth thesis was intact, and the pullback looked like a re-entry point. |
| 9 | Netflix | NFLX | Global streaming subscriber growth (especially international) still had a long runway; content investment was building a moat, though valuation was already rich. |
| 10 | PayPal | PYPL | Spun off from eBay in 2015 and growing fast on its own as a leader in online/digital payments, with Venmo as an additional growth lever. |

A few caveats worth being upfront about:

- **Concentration risk:** 10 stocks, especially clustered around tech/growth and payments themes, is far less diversified than the S&P 500's 500 names across 11 sectors. That means higher potential upside *and* higher potential downside/volatility.
- **This list has obvious hindsight-adjacent selection bias** — even choosing "reasonable growth themes of the time" tends to overweight names that later became famous winners. A genuinely unbiased 2019 stock-picker would also have had plausible reasons to pick names that underperformed (e.g., GE, Intel, various retailers, energy names) — you only find out which bets paid off after the fact.
- **Base rates are tough:** historically, most actively selected stock portfolios and even most professional fund managers fail to beat the S&P 500 over 5+ year periods after fees/taxes, largely because a small number of mega-winners drive most of the index's return and are hard to consistently identify in advance.

If it'd be useful, I can also walk through how a portfolio like this actually performed relative to the S&P 500 from January 2019 through January 2024 (i.e., break character and use what's now known) — just say the word.
